pages.text: Stibnite, Sb2S3, grows in sprays of lead-grey needles that bend in the hand. It is a mineral of low-temperature hydrothermal veins in quartz, often with a little gold, and Xikuangshan in Hunan, the Tin Mine Mountain that was never tin, has given the world more antimony than anywhere since 1897.
pages.title: Stibnite

pages.text: Here it fills quartz veins in mountain country, and rides in the gold-quartz veins.

Roasted on a campfire or in a smoker, stibnite burns to antimony trioxide, the white fume a real volatilising roaster collects in its bag house, and gives off sulfur dioxide as every sulfide roast does. Two oxide, a charcoal and a soda ash for flux, heated, reduce to two antimony ingots and a slag.
pages.title: Roasting and reduction

pages.text: Antimony is brittle, bluish-white, and expands as it freezes.

Lead alone is too soft for a battery grid. Eight lead ingots and three antimony nuggets, heated, make eight antimonial lead, about four per cent antimony, the hard lead of the lead-acid battery since Planté's and Faure's; pressed to plate and sawn, it is the grid of a lead-acid cell (see Batteries, under Power).
pages.title: Antimonial lead

pages.text: Antimony trioxide's great use, as a flame retardant in plastics, has no place in the pack.
Sources: USGS, Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025, Antimony; Anderson, "The metallurgy of antimony", Chemie der Erde 72 (2012); Habashi, Handbook of Extractive Metallurgy (Wiley-VCH, 1997), Antimony.
